'''Gerald Hatten Buss''' (January 27, 1933&nbsp;– February 18, 2013) was an American businessman, [[real estate investor|investor]], chemist, and philanthropist. He was the majority owner of the [[Los Angeles Lakers]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA), winning 10 [[NBA Finals|league championships]] that were highlighted by the team's [[Showtime (basketball)|Showtime era]] during the 1980s. He was inducted into the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]] as a contributor. Buss owned other professional sports franchises in Southern California.

==Early life and business career==
Born in [[Salt Lake City]], Buss and his three younger siblings were raised by their divorced mother, Jessie, who worked as a waitress. His father, Lydus, was an accountant who went on to teach statistics at Berkeley, who abandoned Buss after his first birthday and never returned.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Lakers' Jeanie Buss: She's Got Balls - Sports Illustrated Vault|url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1998/11/02/shes-got-balls-will-jeanie-buss-daughter-of-lakers-owner-jerry-buss-be-the-next-to-rule-her-fathers-sports-kingdom-or-will-one-of-her-brothers-rise-to-power-a-fractured-family-fable|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200922050851/https://vault.si.com/vault/1998/11/02/shes-got-balls-will-jeanie-buss-daughter-of-lakers-owner-jerry-buss-be-the-next-to-rule-her-fathers-sports-kingdom-or-will-one-of-her-brothers-rise-to-power-a-fractured-family-fable|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 22, 2020|access-date=October 23, 2020|newspaper=Sports Illustrated }}</ref> When he was nine years old, Buss moved with his mother to [[Los Angeles]]; three years later when she remarried, they then moved to [[Kemmerer, Wyoming]] and lived in a six-room home with his half-brother Mickey, his half-sister Susan, and stepbrother Jim.<ref name="Shelburne">{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/los-angeles/nba/story/_/id/8959319/los-angeles-lakers-owner-jerry-buss-had-vision-unlike-other|title=Jerry Buss: A true sports visionary|last=Shelburne|first=Ramona|date=February 19, 2013|publisher=[[ESPN.com|ESPNLosAngeles.com]]|access-date=February 21, 2013}}</ref> One of Buss' boyhood jobs was working for his stepfather, Cecil Brown, who owned a plumbing business. Other jobs in Buss' high school days included carrying bags at the [[Kemmerer Hotel]] (paid $2 per day (~$24.08 as of 2025), setting pins at the bowling alley, working on the [[Union Pacific Railroad]], selling stamps, and shining shoes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Van Noll |first=William |date=February 18, 2013 |title=Lakers Legendary Jerry Buss and His "Rags to Riches" Story Truly One of a Kind |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1534466-lakers-legendary-jerry-buss-and-his-rags-to-riches-story-truly-one-of-a-kind |access-date=December 6, 2023 |website=Bleacher Report}}</ref>

Buss earned a scholarship to the [[University of Wyoming]],<ref name="nytobit">{{Cite web |last=Goldstein |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Goldstein (writer, born 1942) |date=February 18, 2013 |title=Jerry Buss, Lakers Owner and Innovator, Dies at 80 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/02/19/sports/basketball/jerry-buss-longtime-lakers-owner-is-dead-at-80.html |access-date=December 6, 2023 |website=The New York Times |language=en-US}}</ref> graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] degree in two and a half years in 1953.  He then returned to Los Angeles and attended the [[University of Southern California]] (USC), where he earned an [[Master of Science|MS]] and [[PhD]] in [[physical chemistry]] in 1957 at the age of 24.<ref name=USC011508>[http://www.usc.edu/uscnews/stories/14720.html Jerry Buss Gives $7.5M to USC College] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080118064857/http://www.usc.edu/uscnews/stories/14720.html |date=January 18, 2008 }}, USC News, January 15, 2008.</ref> Upon completion of his PhD, Buss moved to Boston and worked for [[Arthur D. Little]]. Buss started as a chemist for the [[United States Bureau of Mines|Bureau of Mines]] (now the Mine Safety and Health Administration);<ref>[http://www.uwyo.edu/profiles/notable-alumni/buss.html "Jerry Buss - 1953"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190917111328/http://www.uwyo.edu/profiles/notable-alumni/buss.html |date=September 17, 2019 }}, ''University of Wyoming''. Accessed January 8, 2016.</ref> he then briefly worked in the [[aerospace industry]] for [[McDonnell Douglas]] and was on the faculty of USC's chemistry department.

Buss originally invested in real estate to provide supplementary income so he could continue teaching. His first investment was $1,000 in a 14-unit [[Westside (Los Angeles County)|West Los Angeles]] apartment building in 1959.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jares  |first=Sue Ellen  |date=February 11, 1980 |title=Whether It's the L.A. Lakers or a Lovely Woman, Jerry Buss Is Interested in Champions |url=https://people.com/archive/whether-its-the-l-a-lakers-or-a-lovely-woman-jerry-buss-is-interested-in-champions-vol-13-no-6/ |access-date=April 11, 2019 |language=en |newspaper=People}}</ref> Finding great success in the real estate business, he, along with longtime business partner, Frank Mariani, formed real estate investment company Mariani-Buss Associates.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gloster |first=Rob |date=February 19, 2013 |title=Jerry Buss, Lakers' Owner for 10 NBA Championships, Dies at 80 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2013-02-18/jerry-buss-los-angeles-lakers-owner-during-dynasty-dies-at-79 |access-date=April 9, 2024 |website=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1979, Buss purchased [[Pickfair]], the Beverly Hills estate once owned by [[Mary Pickford]] and [[Douglas Fairbanks]];<ref name="USC011508"/> he sold it in 1987.<ref>daughter-of-lakers-owner-jerry-buss-be-the-next-to-rule-her-fathers-sports-kingdom-or-will-one-of-her-brothers-rise-to-power-a-fractured-family-fable</ref> Buss claimed his company owned—across Arizona, California and Nevada—roughly 700 properties by 1979.

In 1974, Buss produced a movie named ''[[Black Eye (film)|Black Eye]]'' starring former gridiron star [[Fred Williamson|Fred "the Hammer" Williamson]].

Buss was an owner of the [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]] location of the [[Playboy Club]].

===Sports team ownership===
Buss became an owner of the [[Los Angeles Strings (1974–1978)|Los Angeles Strings]] in [[World Team Tennis]].{{when|date=July 2023}} On May 29, 1979, he purchased the [[Los Angeles Lakers]] of the [[NBA]], the [[Los Angeles Kings]] of the [[NHL]], [[The Forum (Inglewood)|The Forum]], and a 13,000-acre ranch in the [[Sierra Nevada]] from [[Jack Kent Cooke]] for $67.5 million (equivalent to ${{Inflation|US|67.5|1979|r=-1}}&nbsp;million in {{Inflation/year|US}}).<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 30, 1979 |title=Cooke, Buss Confirm Sale of Coast Teams |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/05/30/archives/cooke-buss-confirm-sale-of-coast-teams.html |access-date=March 8, 2022 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Noll |first=William Van |date=February 18, 2013 |title=Lakers Legendary Jerry Buss and His "Rags to Riches" Story Truly One of a Kind |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1534466-lakers-legendary-jerry-buss-and-his-rags-to-riches-story-truly-one-of-a-kind |access-date=April 11, 2019 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Lakers owner Jerry Buss dies|url=https://www.foxnews.com/sports/lakers-owner-jerry-buss-dies/|access-date=February 21, 2013|newspaper=Fox News|date=February 18, 2013}}</ref> Buss later sold his controlling interest in the Kings to [[Bruce McNall]] in 1988. He then reached a major advertising agreement with [[Great Western Bank (1919–1997)|Great Western Bank]] for the [[naming rights]] to The Forum, resulting in the official name of the building being changed to the [[Great Western Forum]].

Later, when the [[Women's National Basketball Association|WNBA]] was formed in 1996, Buss took charge of operating that league's Los Angeles franchise, the [[Los Angeles Sparks]]. Eventually, all three teams moved into a more modern arena in downtown Los Angeles, the [[Staples Center]], which opened in 1999. As part of the deal to move the Lakers into Staples Center, Buss sold the Great Western Forum (which was later reverted to its original name).

The Lakers were very successful under Buss' ownership, winning 10 NBA championships with such players as [[Kareem Abdul-Jabbar]], [[Magic Johnson]], [[James Worthy]], [[Shaquille O'Neal]], [[Kobe Bryant]], and [[Pau Gasol]], and with coaches [[Paul Westhead]],  [[Pat Riley]] and [[Phil Jackson]]. He inspired the Lakers' [[Showtime (basketball)|Showtime era]] with his vision that basketball games must be entertaining.<ref>{{cite news|last=Ostler|first=Scott|title=Remembering Jerry Buss and 'Showtime'|url=http://www.sfgate.com/sports/ostler/article/Remembering-Jerry-Buss-and-Showtime-4288541.php|access-date=February 21, 2013|newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle|date=February 19, 2013}}</ref>  The Sparks also experienced their share of success, winning two WNBA championships with such players as [[Lisa Leslie]], [[Tamecka Dixon]] and [[DeLisha Milton-Jones]].

In 2002, when the WNBA was restructured to give its teams individual owners, Buss took ownership of the Sparks. He sold the team in 2006. Buss also owned the [[Los Angeles Lazers]] of the [[Major Soccer League|Major Indoor Soccer League]]. The Lazers also played in The Forum. The team folded in 1989 and the league folded three years later.

His contributions to basketball were recognized by his induction into the [[Basketball Hall of Fame]] in 2010.<ref name="HOF release">{{cite press release|url=http://www.hoophall.com/news/2010/4/5/naismith-memorial-basketball-hall-of-fame-announces-class-of.html |title=Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame Announces Class of 2010 |publisher=Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame |date=April 5, 2010 |access-date=April 5, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100409151224/http://www.hoophall.com/news/2010/4/5/naismith-memorial-basketball-hall-of-fame-announces-class-of.html |archive-date=April 9, 2010 }}</ref> Buss received the Golden Plate Award from the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]] in 1983.<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url= https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#sports}}</ref>

== Philanthropy ==
In January 2008, Buss donated $7.5 million to USC's Department of Chemistry to fund two endowed chairs and an endowed scholarship fund for chemistry graduate students; the two chairs were to be named after his mentors at USC, Professors Sidney Benson and David Dows. Buss was an inaugural member of the USC College Board of Councilors.<ref name="USC011508"/>

His philanthropy also extended to people associated with the Lakers. When former Lakers player [[Walt Hazzard]], then an adviser to the team, suffered a catastrophic stroke in 1996, Buss kept Hazzard on the payroll and told Hazzard's son that his father would remain a Lakers employee for as long as Buss owned the team. When Hazzard died in 2011, he was still a Lakers employee.<ref name=Shelburne/>

==Personal life==
Buss has seven known children. His marriage to JoAnn Mueller ended in divorce in 1972 after having five children: Lee (born 1953),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/lee-klose-inside-jerry-buss-174059360.html|title=Who Is Lee Klose? Inside Jerry Buss’ First Child Who Was Put Up for Adoption|work=Essentially Sports|via=Yahoo! Sports|first=Adrija|last= Mahato|date= January 21, 2026|accessdate=August 18, 2026}}</ref> [[Johnny Buss|Johnny]] (born 1956), [[Jim Buss|Jim]] (born 1959), [[Jeanie Buss|Jeanie]] (born 1961) and Janie (born 1963).<ref name=nytobit/><ref name=LATimesAllInFamily>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120305233234/http://www.latimes.com/la-mag-may032009-goodsport,0,5925924,full.story#axzz2krm7nI61 Los Angeles Times: "All in the Family - If Jerry Buss has his way, the Lakers will belong to his kids" by John Ireland] May 3, 2009</ref><ref name=kahn_11052022>{{cite web|first=Carol|last=Kahn|title=Lee Klose finds birth family after decades|date=November 5, 2022|work=Sedona Red Rock News|url=http://www.redrocknews.com/2022/11/05/klose-finds-birth-family-after-decades/|access-date=November 16, 2022}}</ref> Their oldest child, Lee, was put up for adoption shortly after birth, and did not reunite with her mother and siblings until after Buss's death.<ref name=kahn_11052022/> Buss allegedly married his second wife, Veronica Hoff,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/35786699/santa_cruz_sentinel/ | title=Article clipped from Santa Cruz Sentinel | newspaper=Santa Cruz Sentinel | date=April 15, 1983 | page=12 }}</ref> in 1972 while still married to his first wife, JoAnn. During his time as Lakers owner, Buss was widely known as a [[Playboy lifestyle|playboy]] and had a string of young girlfriends.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dilbeck |first=Steve |date=February 18, 2013 |title=Dodgers affected by Jerry Buss like no other non-NBA team |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/dodgers/la-xpm-2013-feb-18-la-sp-dn-affected-by-buss-20130218-story.html |access-date=April 2, 2024 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> Buss dated Debbie Zafrani, a Playboy bunny and the younger sister of the wife of Lakers player [[Kurt Rambis]].

Buss had two more children with a girlfriend, Karen Demel: Joey (born 1985) and [[Jesse Buss|Jesse]] (born 1988). At the time of his death in 2013, six out of seven of his children worked in the Lakers organization.<ref name="Shelburne" />

In 1990, Buss reached a [[out-of-court settlement|settlement out of court]] in a [[palimony]] suit filed by Puppi Buss, who said that she had an on-and-off relationship with Buss for 15 years, and also alleged that he fathered her son;<ref name="puppi">{{cite news|title=Puppi, Jerry Buss Settle Palimony Suit |date=March 28, 1990 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-03-28-me-289-story.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131222072743/http://articles.latimes.com/1990-03-28/local/me-289_1_jerry-buss |archive-date=December 22, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Nba Jordan Unhurt In Crash |date=July 17, 1987 |newspaper=Sun-Sentinel |url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1987-07-17/sports/8702280652_1_puppi-buss-palimony-suit-summer-games |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216215343/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1987-07-17/sports/8702280652_1_puppi-buss-palimony-suit-summer-games |archive-date=December 16, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> details of the settlement were not revealed.<ref name="puppi" />

On May 29, 2007, Buss was issued a citation for [[driving under the influence]] after two [[California Highway Patrol]] officers saw him driving his gold [[Mercedes-Benz]] on the wrong side of the road in the coastal community of [[Carlsbad, California|Carlsbad]] in northern [[San Diego County, California|San Diego County]], with a 23-year-old woman passenger. After failing a field sobriety test, Buss was taken into custody, given a blood test, and booked on suspicion of driving while intoxicated with a blood-alcohol level over 0.08.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=2886160 |title=Buss also booked for driving with BAC of 0.08 or higher |access-date=January 8, 2008 |date=May 29, 2007 |work=ESPN |publisher=Associated Press |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071009112501/http://sports.espn.go.com/nba/news/story?id=2886160 |archive-date=October 9, 2007 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Buss was a high-stakes cash game [[poker]] player for many years, but later in life was more active in tournament games. His best finishes included third in the [[1991 World Series of Poker]] seven-card stud event and second place in the 2003 [[World Poker Tour]] Freeroll invitational. He also appeared in the [[Game Show Network|GSN]] series ''[[High Stakes Poker]]'' and the [[NBC]] late-night series ''[[Poker After Dark]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.recentpoker.com/articles/bad-fold-51710.html|title=A Bad Fold by David Grey on Poker After Dark|publisher=RecentPoker|access-date=February 3, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110104100812/http://www.recentpoker.com/articles/bad-fold-51710.html|archive-date=January 4, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Buss began collecting coins when he was 10 in Los Angeles. During his life, he acquired three rare US coins: a [[1913 Liberty Head nickel]], an [[1894-S Barber dime]], and an [[1804 dollar]]. He sold his collection at auction in 1985.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gilkes |first1=Paul |title=Coins just one of many interests for Buss |url=https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/coins-just-one-of-many-interests-for-buss.html |website=[[Coin World]] |access-date=November 16, 2025 |date=February 24, 2013}}</ref>

Beginning in the early 1980s, Jerry Buss was seen in and around Los Angeles at charitable events with a group of close friends who were dubbed in the press as “The Seven Dwarfs”.  This group included Jerry's personal friends John Rockwell, Ron and David Wilder, Miguel A. Nunez, Lance Davis, Mark Fulton, and Brian J. Sadler. The Seven Dwarfs would often bid on charitable auction items that would help the causes of the events they attended. The Dwarfs were gifted championship rings when the Lakers won titles and were granted access to all Laker home games and events at the Fabulous Forum / Great Western Forum / Staples Center. Professionally, The Dwarfs positions included special assistant, financial advisor, investment banker, and ADPAC marketing executive. The Dwarfs were regular fixtures in and among the Showtime Lakers throughout the 1980s and 1990s, and until Jerry’s passing in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-21 |title=Whittier Daily News |url=https://www.whittierdailynews.com/ |access-date=2026-08-21 |website=Whittier Daily News |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Death==
In 2012, Buss was in a hospital for months with an undisclosed intestinal problem.<ref>{{cite news|last=Reilly |first=Rick |title=Nash, Lakers still searching |date=January 25, 2013 |work=ESPN.com |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/story/_/id/8880530/steve-nash-lakers-struggling |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130125200025/http://espn.go.com/espn/story/_/id/8880530/steve-nash-lakers-struggling |archive-date=January 25, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> Through his 80th birthday on January 27, 2013, he had not attended a Lakers game during the [[2012–13 Los Angeles Lakers season|2012–13 season]] due to health concerns.<ref>{{cite news|title=Kobe Bryant, Steve Nash help Lakers hold on for 2nd straight win |date=January 27, 2013 |agency=Associated Press |work=ESPN.com |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/recap?gameId=400278373 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130130014838/http://scores.espn.go.com/nba/recap?gameId=400278373 |archive-date=January 30, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> On February 14, 2013, four days before his death, it was revealed that Buss had cancer since 2012.<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130411055753/http://www.lakersnation.com/breaking-news-lakers-owner-jerry-buss-dying-of-cancer/2013/02/14|title=Breaking News: Lakers Owner Jerry Buss Dying Of Cancer}}</ref>

After being hospitalized at [[Cedars-Sinai Medical Center]] with an undisclosed form of cancer, he died of kidney failure on February 18, 2013, aged 80.<ref>{{cite web|last=Lloyd|first=Jonathan|url=http://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/sports/Jerry-Buss-LA-Lakers-Owner-Death-191677081.html|title=Lakers Owner Jerry Buss Dies at Age 80, Leaving Behind "Unparalleled Legacy"|publisher=NBC Bay Area|date=January 27, 1933|access-date=February 19, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Wharton|first=David|url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/lakersnow/la-sp-ln-lakers-jerry-buss-obit-20130214,0,5024446.story|title=Lakers owner Jerry Buss dies|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=February 19, 2013|date=February 18, 2013}}</ref> On February 21, hundreds of friends, colleagues, and family members gathered to pay tribute to Buss in a televised memorial service at the [[Nokia Theatre L.A. Live]], across from the Lakers' home court, [[Staples Center]].<ref name="DN Mem 20130221">{{cite web|last=Painter|first=Jill|title=Jill Painter: Lakers lose innovative owner, L.A. loses friend|url=http://www.dailynews.com/news/ci_22642598/jill-painter-lakers-lose-innovative-owner-l-loses|publisher=The Daily News, Los Angeles|access-date=July 4, 2013|location=Los Angeles, CA|date=February 21, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130529201146/http://www.dailynews.com/news/ci_22642598/jill-painter-lakers-lose-innovative-owner-l-loses|archive-date=May 29, 2013}}</ref> Buss was buried on February 22 at [[Forest Lawn Memorial Park (Hollywood Hills)|Forest Lawn Memorial Park]] in [[Hollywood Hills]] in a private ceremony with family and close friends.<ref name="HP Burial 20130222">{{cite news|last=Associated Press|title=Jerry Buss Buried At Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Hollywood Hills In Private Ceremony| url = https://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/02/22/jerry-buss-buried_n_2746472.html|work=Huffington Post|access-date=July 4, 2013|location=Los Angeles|date=February 22, 2013}}</ref>

NBA commissioner [[David Stern]] said of Buss "The NBA has lost a visionary owner whose influence on our league is incalculable and will be felt for decades to come".<ref>{{cite news|url=http://nba.si.com/2013/02/18/jerry-buss-dies-nba-reaction|title=NBA world reacts to Jerry Buss' death|publisher=Nba.si.com|access-date=February 19, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130221034727/http://nba.si.com/2013/02/18/jerry-buss-dies-nba-reaction/|archive-date=February 21, 2013}}</ref> Lakers guard [[Kobe Bryant]] said "His impact is felt worldwide," and called Buss "the greatest owner in sports ever".<ref>{{cite news|last=Beacham|first=Greg|url=http://www.miamiherald.com/2013/02/18/3240846/jerry-buss-the-los-angeles-lakers.html|title=LOS ANGELES: Jerry Buss, Lakers' flamboyant owner, dies at 80|publisher=MiamiHerald.com|date=August 14, 2009|access-date=February 19, 2013}}</ref>

{{anchor|Trust}}Buss's 66% controlling ownership of the Lakers passed to his six children (Johnny, Jim, Jeanie, Janie, Joey, and Jesse) via a trust, with each child receiving an equal vote (11% for each child).<ref name=markazi_02182013>{{cite news|last=Markazi |first=Arash |title=Buss family won't sell Lakers |date=February 18, 2013 |work=ESPN.com |url=https://www.espn.com/los-angeles/nba/story/_/id/8960441/family-jerry-buss-maintain-los-angeles-lakers-ownership |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130219155444/http://espn.go.com/los-angeles/nba/story/_/id/8960441/family-jerry-buss-maintain-los-angeles-lakers-ownership |archive-date=February 19, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Bresnahan |first=Mike |title=Buss family faces crucial moment with the Lakers |date=April 19, 2014 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/basketball/nba/lakers/la-sp-lakers-buss-family-20140420,0,1940758,full.story |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140420111025/http://www.latimes.com/sports/basketball/nba/lakers/la-sp-lakers-buss-family-20140420,0,1940758,full.story |archive-date=April 20, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> His succession plan had daughter [[Jeanie Buss|Jeanie]] assume his previous title as the Lakers' governor as well as its team representative at NBA Board of Governors meetings.<ref name=markazi_02182013/><ref name=bresnahan_02192013>{{cite news|last=Bresnahan |first=Mike |title=Lakers expected to remain a Buss family-owned team |date=February 19, 2013 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/sports/basketball/nba/lakers/la-sp-lakers-ownership-20130219,0,6689307.story |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130220005530/http://www.latimes.com/sports/basketball/nba/lakers/la-sp-lakers-ownership-20130219,0,6689307.story |archive-date=February 20, 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[2013 World Series of Poker]] paid tribute to Buss before the $2,500 Seven Card Stud event.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pokernews.com/tours/wsop/2013-world-series-of-poker/event-23-2-500-seven-card-stud/photos.2833.htm|title=WSOP Tribute to Dr. Jerry Buss|date=June 12, 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230831125936/https://www.pokernews.com/tours/wsop/2013-world-series-of-poker/event-23-2-500-seven-card-stud/photos.2833.htm|archive-date=August 31, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsop.com/news/2013/Jun/4373/KOBE-BRYANT-HAS-A-SPECIAL-MESSAGE-FOR-THE-SEVEN-CARD-STUD-FIELD.html|title=KOBE BRYANT HAS A SPECIAL MESSAGE FOR THE SEVEN CARD STUD FIELD|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230831125918/https://www.wsop.com/news/2013/Jun/4373/KOBE-BRYANT-HAS-A-SPECIAL-MESSAGE-FOR-THE-SEVEN-CARD-STUD-FIELD.html|archive-date=August 31, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>
